Dynamic specification

Source: R/dynamic.R
psp_dynamic.Rd

Adds observed state dependence to psprobit() / psoprobit(): the previous period's outcome \(y_{i,t-1}\) and, optionally, its spatial lag \((W y_{t-1})_i\) enter the latent equation as regressors. The first period is used only as the initial condition, so estimation uses periods \(2, \dots, T\). For ordered outcomes the lag enters as one indicator per category above the first.

Usage

psp_dynamic(
  lag_y = !latent,
  lag_Wy = FALSE,
  initial = c("wooldridge", "none"),
  latent = FALSE
)

Arguments

lag_y

Logical; include \(y_{i,t-1}\) (columns lag_*).

lag_Wy

Logical; include \((W y_{t-1})_i\) (columns W_lag_*).

initial

"wooldridge" or "none" (treat the first-period outcome as exogenous). Ignored with latent = TRUE.

latent

Logical; latent AR(1) dynamics instead of lagged outcomes.

Value

An object of class psp_dynamic.

Details

With initial = "wooldridge" (the default) the random effects are modelled as \(\alpha_i = \psi' y_{i1} + \bar x_i'\pi + a_i\) (Wooldridge 2005): the first-period outcome (columns init_*) and the unit means of all regressors over the estimation periods (columns mean_*) are added to the model. This handles the initial-conditions problem of dynamic random-effects models.

Impacts of the regressors are short-run (within-period) impacts.

With latent = TRUE the dynamics act on the latent outcome instead, \(z_t = \rho W z_t + \gamma z_{t-1} + X_t\beta + \alpha + u_t\) (Wang and Kockelman 2009). The coefficient \(\gamma\) is reported as lag_z. Every period is modelled; the first has no lagged term, so its latent outcome serves as the initial condition and shares the random effect with the later periods (no separate initial-conditions device is needed). Probabilities, impacts and predictions integrate over the latent history, and psp_response_path() gives the propagation of a shock. Latent dynamics need time-invariant weights and cannot be combined with lagged outcomes. \(\gamma\) mixes slowly against \(\rho\) (it is drawn given the latent values), so plan on longer chains than for static models and check the convergence diagnostics.

References

Wang, X. and Kockelman, K. M. (2009). Bayesian inference for ordered response data with a dynamic spatial-ordered probit model. Journal of Regional Science 49, 877-913.

Wooldridge, J. M. (2005). Simple solutions to the initial conditions problem in dynamic, nonlinear panel data models with unobserved heterogeneity. Journal of Applied Econometrics 20, 39-54.

Examples

W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(5, 5), style = "W")
d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 6, beta = c(-0.3, 1, -1), rho = 0.3, gamma = 0.8, seed = 1)
fit <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, d, c("id", "time"), W, dynamic = psp_dynamic(),
                impacts = FALSE,
                control = psp_control(iter = 300, warmup = 200, chains = 1, seed = 1))
#> Warning: Possible convergence problems (R-hat > 1.01 or bulk ESS < 100) for: (Intercept), x1, x2, lag_y, init_y, mean_x1, mean_x2, rho, sigma_alpha. Consider more iterations.
coef(fit)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2       lag_y      init_y     mean_x1 
#>  -0.7604611   1.3051023  -1.3946623   2.0093651  -0.2378243   1.2928919 
#>     mean_x2         rho sigma_alpha 
#>   1.5797796   0.1889955   1.3583197
